intervention.description: investigation of magnetic structure by accounting for longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature

structure.description: face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures

evidence_units.mechanism: LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni
evidence_spans: Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni.

intervention.description: investigation of phase stability and stacking fault energy by accounting for longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs)

evidence_units.mechanism: LSFs impact phase stability and stacking fault energy; hcp phase becomes energetically preferable at cryogenic temperatures, resulting in negative stacking fault energy
evidence_spans: The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions.

intervention.description: investigation of stacking fault energy and nano-twin formation by accounting for longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) with increasing temperature

evidence_units.mechanism: With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins
evidence_spans: With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins.

intervention.description: Accounting for local spin fluctuations (LSFs) at finite temperature

structure.description: Mean magnetic moments { m I } induced for alloy components

evidence_units.mechanism: Finite magnetic moments thermally induced for Cr, Ni and Co at all volumes even at the lowest temperature considered here (50 K) in both the fcc and hcp phases due to LSFs

outcome.direction: finite moments induced where previously zero

comparison.direction: Cr, Ni and Co moments zero in FS

evidence_spans: Accounting for the LSFs at finite temperature (contour plots in Fig. 1 ), finite magnetic moments have been thermally induced for Cr, Ni and Co at all volumes even at the lowest temperature considered here (50 K) in both the fcc and hcp phases.

intervention.action: LSF calculation with thermal lattice expansion
intervention.description: Mean magnetic moments { m I } as function of temperature with experimental thermal lattice expansion

structure.description: Mean magnetic moments { m I } in both phases

evidence_units.mechanism: Mean magnetic moments { m I } in both phases significantly increase with temperature
evidence_spans: Taking the experimentally determined thermal lattice expansion [40] into account (indicated by stars in the contour plots in Fig. 1 ), the mean magnetic moments { m I } as function of temperature are shown in Table 1 for both the fcc and hcp phases. It is evident that { m I } in both phases significantly increase with temperature, and at the given temperatures the magnetic states of the alloy components in the fcc phase are very close to those in the hcp phase. At 100 K, the difference in m I between the two phases amounts to ~0.05, 0.03, 0.17 and 0.23 μ B for Co, Cr, Fe, and Mn, respectively, and this difference slightly reduces with increasing temperature. Furthermore, m Ni in the two phases is almost identical at the considered temperatures with difference less than 0.005 μ B .

intervention.description: Free energy differences between the fcc and hcp phases

evidence_units.mechanism: LSFs at finite temperature systemically lower the absolute magnitude of Δ F fcc→hcp and promote rather smooth dependencies on volume and temperature; the partial contributions to Δ F fcc→hcp , i.e., the magnetic entropy and internal energy, may be considerably altered by LSFs at finite temperature

outcome.property: Critical temperature of fcc-hcp phase transition

evidence_spans: With respect to the Δ F fcc→hcp derived from the FS calculations, the LSFs at finite temperature systemically lower the absolute magnitude of Δ F fcc→hcp , and promote rather smooth dependencies of Δ F fcc→hcp on volume and temperature, as indicated by straight contour lines. As detailed in Fig. 1 , the noticeable changes in the shape of contour lines in the FS calculations [indicated by the arrows in panel (a)] emerge from the distinct { μ 0 I } in the fcc and hcp phases, amplified by temperature in the calculation of magnetic entropy. These changes are significantly eliminated by the gradually varying { m I } induced via LSFs in both the fcc and hcp phases. That is, the partial contributions to Δ F fcc→hcp , i.e., the magnetic entropy and internal energy, may be considerably altered by LSFs at finite temperature (see Fig. 3 ). Nevertheless, LSFs yield small influence on the phase boundary (defined here as Δ F fcc→hcp = 0) of PM CoCrFeMnNi. Referring to the experimental volumes [40] indicated by stars, the critical temperature of fcc-hcp phase transition at ambient pressure is determined to be ~430 K in the LSF calculations, compared to ~438 K in the FS calculations.
limitations: explicit phonon effect is not considered in the present theory

intervention.action: LSF methodology application for finite-temperature magnetic state description
intervention.description: Used root-mean-square magnetic moment m_I(w,T) and fluctuating medium approximation to determine {m_I} at finite temperature.

parameters.theory_framework: DFT via EMTO with PBE functional
parameters.volume_assumption: finite-temperature volume of hcp identical to fcc

structure.description: Finite-temperature magnetic state in fcc and hcp phases

evidence_units.mechanism: Finite-temperature properties derived from free energy F_alpha(w,T) = E_int(w,{M_I}) - TS_mag({M_I}), where E_int approximated by DLM paramagnet total energy and S_mag evaluated via mean-field expression, allowing evaluation of fcc-hcp phase stability and stacking fault energy.

outcome.measurement_method: comparison with experimental and calculated properties from literature [29]-[30], [34], [39]

comparison.baseline_material: bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy

evidence_spans: The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA.

The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.
limitations: Structural relaxation in the faulted supercell was omitted

intervention.action: LSF calculation with thermal lattice expansion
intervention.description: Intrinsic stacking fault energy γ_isf as function of volume and temperature

structure.description: Thermodynamic stability of hcp phase relative to fcc at low temperatures

candidate.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures the fcc phase would remain metastable, because of, e.g., high kinetic barriers [16] , [43] , and formation of nano-twins and stacking faults therein is energetically preferable due to negative γ_isf

comparison.direction: LSF values lower than FS values in most fcc-stable region

evidence_spans: Taking the experimentally determined lattice expansion (indicated by the stars) into account, the γ_isf of PM CoCrFeMnNi is predicted from the LSF calculations to increase from -17 mJ m^-2 at 50 K, reach zero at ~260 K and keep rising to 31 mJ m^-2 at 1000 K, which are contrasted with -19 mJ m^-2 , ~290 K and 36 mJ m^-2 , respectively, from the FS calculations. The positive temperature dependence of γ_isf predicted here is comparable with that reported by Huang et al . [42] . Nevertheless, the magnitudes of γ_isf accounting for LSFs are lower than those found in ref. [42] , because the magnetic contribution determined in the work is significantly reduced owing to LSFs.

In the temperature interval 77–293 K nano-twins and stacking faults were reported in experiments [7] , [10] – [15] , the γ_isf of PM fcc CoCrFeMnNi is predicted to be as low as -15~2 mJ m^-2 when accounting for LSFs and lattice expansion. The low γ_isf is attributed to the fact that the hcp phase is thermodynamically stable to the fcc one at these conditions (see Fig. 2 ). Namely, at cryogenic temperatures the fcc phase would remain metastable, because of, e.g., high kinetic barriers [16] , [43] , and formation of nano-twins and stacking faults therein is energetically preferable. With decreasing temperature, the plastic deformation by nano-twins and stacking faults is enhanced owing to the reduced γ_isf , resulting in a good combination of strength and ductility at cryogenic temperatures as observed in the experiments.

intervention.description: fcc-hcp interfacial energy σ as function of temperature

structure.description: Interfacial energy between fcc and hcp phases

candidate.mechanism: LSFs at finite temperature slightly lower σ
evidence_spans: Extrapolating our calculations to 0 K, the σ of PM CoCrFeMnNi is predicted to be ~6.1 and 7.0 mJ m^-2 in the LSF and FS schemes, respectively, showing a good consistency with the values calculated for Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic stainless steels by Li et al . [44] , i.e., 7.5–9.0 mJ m^-2 at 0 K.

In the temperature interval 50–1200 K, the σ of PM CoCrFeMnNi is estimated to slightly vary in the range of ~3.1–6.0 and 3.6–6.8 mJ m^-2 for the LSF and FS calculations, respectively. Therefore, the error bar of γ_isf associated with using the constant σ equal to 5 mJ m^-2 is expected to be less than 4 mJ m^-2 for both the LSF and FS calculations.

intervention.description: Calculated stacking fault energy (gamma_isf_SC) assuming magnetic state of atomic layers nearest to the intrinsic stacking fault is same as in hcp structure while remaining layers treated as fcc.

candidate.mechanism: The fcc-hcp interfacial energy sigma was determined by comparing results from the thermodynamic model with the supercell calculations via the relation 2 sigma = gamma_isf_SC - 2 Delta F_fcc->hcp / A.

outcome.measurement_method: calculated via relation 2 sigma = gamma_isf_SC - 2 Delta F_fcc->hcp / A

limitations: Structural relaxation in the faulted supercell was omitted
evidence_spans: The fcc-hcp interfacial energy sigma was determined by comparing the results from the thermodynamic model [41] with the supercell calculations via 2 sigma = gamma isf SC - 2 Delta F fcc → hcp / A ( A is the interfacial area per atom).

gamma isf SC is the stacking fault energy calculated using the supercell approach, in which we assumed that the magnetic state of the atomic layers nearest to the intrinsic stacking fault is the same as in the hcp structure, while the remaining layers were treated identically to the fcc case [39] .
